q: Electrical energy can be transformed into a wide variety of other useful forms of energy.
e: Electrical energy is highly versatile and can be converted into many other useful forms of energy.

q: The transformation of electrical energy into heat energy is very useful and important.
e: Many home appliances rely on the useful transformation of electrical energy into heat energy.

q: Electrical energy is provided by sources of electromotive force such as resistors and capacitors.
e: Electrical energy is provided by sources of electromotive force such as batteries and generators.

q: A steady current will flow through the conductor if a steady potential difference is maintained between its ends by using batteries and generators.
e: Batteries and generators maintain the steady potential difference required for a steady current.

q: Batteries and generators are called sources of electromotive force.
e: These devices provide the electromotive force needed to drive current through a circuit.

q: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from electrical form into other forms.
e: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into electrical form.

q: A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy to provide electrical power.
e: The chemical reactions inside a battery generate electrical energy for the circuit.

q: In an electric generator, heat energy is converted into electrical energy.
e: In an electric generator, mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy.

q: A source of electromotive force has a positive terminal and a negative terminal.
e: These terminals define the polarity and direction of the potential difference provided by the source.

q: The positive charges are sent from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.
e: The positive charges are sent from the negative terminal to the positive terminal within the source.

q: The main function of the source is to send negative charges from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.
e: This internal movement of negative charges maintains the potential difference across the terminals.

q: Electromotive force, abbreviated as emf, is the amount of energy provided by the battery per unit charge to move round the complete circuit.
e: This is the exact definition of electromotive force in a complete circuit.

q: Electromotive force is measured in unit of ampere ($A$).
e: Electromotive force is measured in unit of volt ($V$).

q: One volt is equivalent to joule per coulomb of electric charge ($J C^{-1}$).
e: This equivalence defines the volt in terms of energy and charge.

q: Despite its name, electromotive force is actually a physical force.
e: Despite its name, electromotive force is not actually a force; it is a potential energy per unit charge.

q: Generally, a source of electromotive force has an internal resistance.
e: Real-world sources like batteries inherently possess some internal resistance.

q: The internal resistance of a battery depends on its size, chemical properties, life time, and temperature.
e: These physical and chemical factors determine the magnitude of a battery's internal resistance.

q: A battery which has an internal resistance $r$ must be viewed as a resistor of resistance $r$ connected in parallel to the battery.
e: A battery which has an internal resistance $r$ must be viewed as a resistor of resistance $r$ connected in series to the battery.

q: By Ohm's law, the potential difference across the external resistor is $V = IR$.
e: This is the standard application of Ohm's law to the external load resistor.

q: The work done in moving a unit positive charge from one end to another of the internal resistance $r$ of the battery is $Ir$.
e: The voltage drop across the internal resistance is given by the product of current and internal resistance.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is $IR - Ir$.
e: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is $IR + Ir$.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is the emf $E$ of the battery.
e: The sum of the potential drops across the external and internal resistances equals the emf.

q: The circuit equation is $E = I(R - r)$.
e: The circuit equation is $E = I(R + r)$.

q: The potential difference between the terminals of a battery when it is connected to an external circuit is given by $V = E - Ir$.
e: The terminal voltage is the emf minus the voltage drop across the internal resistance.

q: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always greater than its emf.
e: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals is always less than its emf.

q: The potential difference across the terminals of a battery connected to an external circuit is called the terminal voltage (or available voltage) of the battery.
e: This is the voltage actually available to the external circuit.

q: Electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.
e: Electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in an open circuit.

q: Terminal voltage is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.
e: Terminal voltage is measured when current is flowing through a closed circuit.

q: Thus, emf is a closed-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is an open-circuit voltage.
e: Thus, emf is an open-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is a closed-circuit voltage.

q: Charging a battery means the chemical energy of the battery which has been used up is now supplied back by electrical energy from some external source.
e: An external battery charger provides the electrical energy to reverse the chemical reactions.

q: In charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to $E - Ir$.
e: In charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to $E + Ir$.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when open circuit (not in use) is $V = E$.
e: With no current flowing, there is no internal voltage drop, so terminal voltage equals emf.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when charging is $V > E$.
e: During charging, the external source must overcome both the emf and the internal voltage drop.

q: When two or more electromotive sources (batteries) are connected in series, the resultant emf is the algebraic sum of the individual emfs.
e: Series connections combine the voltages algebraically depending on their polarities.

q: In series aiding arrangement, the currents leaving the batteries are in opposite directions.
e: In series aiding arrangement, the currents leaving the batteries are in the same direction.

q: In series aiding, the resultant emf is $E_1 + E_2$.
e: The emfs add together because the batteries are connected with matching polarities in sequence.

q: The total internal resistance of two batteries in series aiding is $r_1 - r_2$.
e: The total internal resistance of two batteries in series is $r_1 + r_2$.

q: Two batteries in series aiding can be regarded as a single battery having an emf $(E_1 + E_2)$ and internal resistance $(r_1 + r_2)$.
e: This equivalent circuit simplifies the analysis of series-aiding battery combinations.

q: In series opposing arrangement, the emfs of the batteries are in the same direction.
e: In series opposing arrangement, the emfs of the batteries are in opposition.

q: The resultant emf in series opposing is the sum of the individual emfs.
e: The resultant emf in series opposing is the difference between the individual emfs.

q: If $E_1$ is greater than $E_2$, the resultant emf of those two batteries in series opposing is $(E_1 - E_2)$.
e: The larger emf dominates, and the net emf is the difference between the two.

q: The total internal resistance of two batteries in series opposing is $r_1 - r_2$.
e: The total internal resistance is still the sum, $r_1 + r_2$, regardless of the emf orientation.

q: In parallel connection of two identical batteries, the opposite polarity terminals of the batteries are connected together.
e: In parallel connection, the same polarity terminals of the batteries must be connected together.

q: The resultant emf of the parallel-combination of two identical batteries is just the emf $E$ of a single battery.
e: Connecting identical batteries in parallel does not increase the total voltage.

q: Since the internal resistances of two identical batteries are in parallel, the resultant internal resistance is $2r$.
e: The resultant internal resistance of two identical resistors in parallel is $r/2$.

q: A parallel combination of two identical batteries can be regarded as a single battery having an emf $E$ and an internal resistance $r/2$.
e: This equivalent circuit provides the same voltage but with a lower internal resistance.

q: In parallel connection of batteries, care must be taken that the terminal of the same polarity should be connected together.
e: Connecting same polarities ensures the batteries work together rather than against each other.

q: If terminals of opposite polarity are connected together in parallel, batteries may be damaged.
e: Connecting opposite polarities in parallel creates a short circuit between the batteries, causing damage.

q: Electrical energy is energy associated with the flow of charge through any part of circuit.
e: This defines the fundamental nature of electrical energy in a circuit.

q: Electrical energy can be generated from source of emf such as batteries, generators, dynamos and photovoltaic cells.
e: These are all common sources that provide electromotive force to generate electrical energy.

q: Electrical energy can be stored in other forms for future application using fuel cells, batteries, capacitors and inductors.
e: These components and devices are capable of storing electrical energy in chemical or electromagnetic fields.

q: The work done $W$ in bringing the amount of charge $Q$ from A to B is $W = Q/V$.
e: The work done $W$ in bringing the amount of charge $Q$ from A to B is $W = QV$.

q: The work done $W$ by the battery in taking the charge $Q$ from A to B is the electrical energy supplied by the battery.
e: The work done on the charge equals the electrical energy transferred to the circuit.

q: The electrical energy supplied by the battery is transformed into heat energy in the resistor $R$.
e: As current passes through the resistor, electrical energy is dissipated as heat.

q: Heat energy is produced because protons collide with the atoms in the resistor $R$ when they pass through it.
e: Heat energy is produced because electrons collide with the atoms in the resistor $R$ when they pass through it.

q: The electrical energy $W$ produced by the battery is $W = VIt$.
e: This is the standard formula for electrical energy using voltage, current, and time.

q: The electrical energy $W$ can also be written as $W = I^2Rt$.
e: Substituting $V = IR$ into $W = VIt$ yields $W = I^2Rt$.

q: The electrical energy $W$ can also be written as $W = V^2 R t$.
e: The electrical energy $W$ can also be written as $W =  rac{V^2}{R}t$.

q: If an electric motor is connected between A and B, the electrical energy will be transformed into mechanical energy.
e: Electric motors are designed to convert electrical energy into mechanical work.

q: The practical unit of electrical energy is kilowatt hour ($kWh$).
e: The kilowatt hour is the standard commercial unit used for billing electrical energy.

q: $1 	ext{ kWh}$ is equal to $3.60 	imes 10^3 	ext{ J}$.
e: $1 	ext{ kWh}$ is equal to $3.60 	imes 10^6 	ext{ J}$.

q: $1 	ext{ kWh} = 1000 	ext{ W} 	imes 1 	ext{ h} = 1000 	imes 60 	imes 60 	ext{ J}$.
e: This calculation correctly converts kilowatts to watts and hours to seconds to find the energy in joules.

q: Electrical power is the total amount of electrical energy transferred.
e: Electrical power is the rate of transfer of electrical energy.

q: If the electrical energy $W$ is transferred in the time $t$, then the electrical power $P$ is $P = W/t$.
e: This is the fundamental definition of power as energy per unit time.

q: The electrical power $P$ can be calculated as $P = VI$.
e: This formula relates power directly to voltage and current.

q: The electrical power $P$ can be calculated as $P = I^2/R$.
e: The electrical power $P$ can be calculated as $P = I^2R$.

q: The unit of electrical power $P$ is the watt ($W$).
e: The watt is the standard SI unit for measuring electrical power.

q: If $1 	ext{ joule (J)}$ of electrical energy is transferred in $1 	ext{ second (s)}$ the electrical power is $1 	ext{ watt (W)}$.
e: This defines the watt in terms of fundamental SI units of energy and time.

q: When electric current passes through a conductor, the electrons in the conductor are accelerated due to electric field.
e: The electric field exerts a force on the free electrons, causing them to accelerate.

q: The electrons collide with the other atoms and gain kinetic energy which appears as heat energy.
e: The electrons collide with the other atoms and lose their kinetic energy which appears as heat energy.

q: The electrical energy $W$ (measured in joule) is related to the amount of heat $H$ (measured in calorie) as $W = JH$.
e: This equation links the electrical work done to the thermal energy produced using Joule's equivalent.

q: $J$ is a constant called Joule's mechanical equivalent of heat.
e: This constant represents the conversion factor between mechanical/electrical work and heat.

q: The value of Joule's mechanical equivalent of heat $J$ is $4.2 	ext{ cal J}^{-1}$.
e: The value of Joule's mechanical equivalent of heat $J$ is $4.2 	ext{ J cal}^{-1}$.

q: The amount of heat $H$ can be calculated as $H =  rac{I^2Rt}{J}$.
e: This formula calculates the heat in calories by dividing the electrical energy in joules by $J$.

q: Joule's law states that the amount of heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the current.
e: Joule's law states that the amount of heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current.

q: Joule's law states that the heat produced is directly proportional to the value of resistance.
e: For a given current and time, a higher resistance will produce more heat.

q: Joule's law states that the heat produced is directly proportional to the time taken by the current to pass through the resistor.
e: The longer the current flows, the more heat energy is generated.

q: The amount of heat $H$ can also be written as $H =  rac{VIt}{J}$.
e: This is an alternative form of Joule's law using voltage, current, and time.

q: The amount of heat $H$ can also be written as $H =  rac{V^2 t}{RJ}$.
e: This form is useful when the voltage across the resistor and its resistance are known.

q: The electrical energy supplied by the battery is transformed into heat energy $H$ in the resistor $R$.
e: This describes the fundamental energy conversion occurring in a resistive heating element.

q: Joule's law of electricity and heat was experimentally studied by James Prescott Joule in 1841.
e: James Prescott Joule established this relationship through his experiments in 1841.

q: Heat energy is produced in the heating coil of Joule's calorimeter.
e: The heating coil acts as the resistor where electrical energy is converted to heat in the calorimeter.

q: The heat $H$ produced is inversely proportional to the square of the current.
e: The heat $H$ produced is directly proportional to the square of the current.

q: In general, most of the electrical energy supplied to a resistor in an electric circuit is converted into heat.
e: Resistors are specifically designed to dissipate electrical energy primarily as heat.

q: The heating effect of electric current has special applications in domestic appliances.
e: Many household devices rely on this heating effect for their primary function.

q: An electric light bulb is made of a glass bulb consisting a copper filament.
e: An electric light bulb is made of a glass bulb consisting of a tungsten filament.

q: A small amount of oxygen, an active gas, is added after the air is removed from the light bulb.
e: A small amount of argon, an inert gas, is added after the air is removed from the light bulb.

q: The tungsten filament becomes hot when a current flows through it.
e: The resistance of the filament causes it to heat up significantly as current passes through.

q: The inert gas increases the evaporation of the filament.
e: The inert gas reduces the evaporation of the filament.

q: The electric light bulb converts most of the electrical energy into heat and light energy.
e: Incandescent bulbs are highly inefficient, converting the majority of their input energy into heat rather than light.

q: In an electric iron, a mica sheet is wound around the nichrome wire.
e: Mica acts as an insulating framework to hold and isolate the heating element.

q: Mica is a good electrical conductor and can withstand very high temperature.
e: Mica is a good electrical insulator and can withstand very high temperature.

q: The heating element in an electric iron is controlled by a thermostat.
e: The thermostat regulates the temperature by managing the power to the heating element.

q: The thermostat switches the current on and off to maintain the selected temperature.
e: This cycling action keeps the iron at a steady, user-defined heat level.

q: An electric iron has an electric power of $15-45 	ext{ W}$.
e: An electric iron has an electric power of $750-1000 	ext{ W}$.

q: In an electric stove, a coil of nichrome wire is placed in the groove of the heat-resistant material.
e: Nichrome is used because of its high resistance and ability to withstand high heating temperatures.

q: An electric stove has an electrical power ranging from $600 	ext{ W}$ to $2000 	ext{ W}$.
e: This high power range is necessary to generate sufficient heat for cooking.

q: A laptop computer typically has an electrical power of $100-250 	ext{ W}$.
e: A laptop computer typically has an electrical power of $15-45 	ext{ W}$.

q: A refrigerator typically has an electrical power of $100-250 	ext{ W}$.
e: This is the standard operating power range for typical household refrigerators.

q: A fuse is a thin short wire of tin-lead alloy.
e: This specific alloy is chosen for its low melting point, allowing it to break the circuit easily.

q: A fuse is used in electric circuits to prevent electrical appliances from being damaged if excessive current flows through them.
e: The fuse acts as a sacrificial safety device to protect the rest of the circuit.

q: The fuse wire is fitted in a glass tube (cartridge) or on a porcelain block.
e: These housings safely contain the fuse wire and any arcing that occurs when it melts.

q: When a current greater than the rated value flows in the circuit, the fuse becomes so hot that it will melt and break the circuit.
e: The heat generated by the excessive current ($I^2Rt$) melts the fuse wire, opening the circuit.

q: For an appliance rated as $700 	ext{ W}$ or less, a $13 	ext{ A}$ fuse should be fitted.
e: For an appliance rated as $700 	ext{ W}$ or less, a $3 	ext{ A}$ fuse should be fitted.

q: For appliances above $700 	ext{ W}$, a $13 	ext{ A}$ fuse should be fitted.
e: Higher wattage appliances draw more current and therefore require a higher-rated fuse.

q: When the fuse melts, the current stops flowing and the electrical appliance in the circuit is not damaged.
e: By breaking the circuit, the fuse prevents overheating and potential fire or damage to the appliance.
